title: Carnival of Souls

evidence.note: A partial scan of the Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures and Filmstrips volume for 1962 (archive.org item) found no entry for 'Carnival of Souls'. The scan did not cover the whole volume, and the specific sections or pages read are not recorded. The archive.org item may not cover all of 1962. Not finding an entry is not proof that no registration exists.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, 1962 (archive.org)

evidence.note: A partial scan of the 1963 motion-pictures volume (archive.org item) also found no entry for 'Carnival of Souls'. The scan did not cover the whole volume, the sections or pages read are not recorded, and the item may not cover all of 1963. Not finding an entry is not proof that no registration exists.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, 1963 (archive.org)

evidence.note: Wikipedia reports that the US release failed to include a copyright notice on the prints, which would automatically place them in the public domain, while the foreign release marketed by Walter Manley carried a copyright card and was protected for overseas sales. No document stating 'no notice' was examined directly, and a renewal search of the Copyright Office public catalog (a 1962 film's renewal window fell in 1990) was not run. The print therefore stays undetermined, even though a partial scan of the 1962 and 1963 catalogs found no registration entry.

The Internet Archive item CarnivalofSouls (runtime 01:22:59) lists creator Herk Harvey, year 1962, and carries the Creative Commons public-domain license URL http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/. This is the uploader's tag, not a rights determination.

Wikipedia credits organist and composer Gene Moore with the original organ score. A score recorded on the film's own track would normally share the print's status, which is itself unconfirmed by a primary record. No separate registration or renewal was checked. A separately released soundtrack recording would be a different work.

John Clifford is credited as the screenwriter. No pre-existing underlying work was identified in the sources fetched, but no primary record was checked. Wikipedia says the 1998 remake's producer, Peter Soby, negotiated rights from Harvey and Clifford.
No active mark was identified, but no trademark database was searched. The 1998 remake, "Wes Craven Presents Carnival of Souls", is a separate work.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright. Slavish copying of public-domain works without originality is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191, S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). Original additions such as a newly composed or recorded score, new titles or subtitles, commentary or other original material can be protected.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - Circumvention of copyright protection systems. Ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break this rule even when the film itself is public domain.

Wikipedia reports that the Criterion Collection issued a 2-disc DVD in 2000 with a 78-minute theatrical version and an 84-minute director's cut, then reissued it in 2016 on DVD and Blu-ray with a new restoration. Any added commentary, subtitles or other original material on those discs may be protected.

editorial:
Carnival of Souls was made for about $33,000, shot in Douglas County, Kansas and Salt Lake City. Herk Harvey directed it from a John Clifford screenplay, with an original organ score by Gene Moore. It premiered on September 26, 1962, at the Granada Theatre in Lawrence, Kansas, with Herts-Lion International as distributor. A reuser wants it because Wikipedia reports the US prints carried no copyright notice, which would put the US release in the public domain, and the Internet Archive hosts a copy tagged public domain.

The rights trap is that this rests on a no-notice report, not on a document. A partial scan of the Catalog of Copyright Entries volumes for 1962 and 1963 found no registration entry for the film. That fits the report but does not prove it, because the whole volumes were not read. No notice-failure document was examined, and the Copyright Office catalog was not searched for a 1990 renewal. Wikipedia also says the foreign release marketed by Walter Manley carried a copyright card and was protected overseas. Score, story and trademark were not checked against primary records. Criterion's 2000 DVD set and 2016 restoration may carry protectable additions, and ripping a copy-protected disc can raise a DMCA issue. The Internet Archive copy is the safer source.
faq: Can I upload or reuse Carnival of Souls?

The print may be usable in the US, but it is not confirmed. The US release is reported to have lacked a copyright notice, and a partial scan of the 1962 and 1963 Catalog of Copyright Entries volumes found no registration entry. That scan is not proof. Foreign releases are reported to have been protected. Use the Internet Archive copy and avoid ripping Criterion discs, which may include protected additions and copy protection.
Is the 1998 remake also public domain?

Nothing here shows that. The 1998 remake, "Wes Craven Presents Carnival of Souls", is a separate work, and Wikipedia says its producer negotiated rights from Harvey and Clifford. Its status was not researched.
